summary.text: For modulus \(550172=196\cdot2807\), the congruence \(2^{r+29400t}\equiv2^r\) reduces the question to finitely many \(r\), and a modular avoidance computation shows that the residue \(63945\) is not attained before \(k=17135927\); a finite residue-class table also supplies eventual coverage, so the least covering index is at least \(17135927\). A bit-sieve shows that more than \(550171\) primes lie below \(8567965\), hence the \(550172\)-nd prime is below that number and \(2(p_{550172}-1)\le17135926\), contradicting the proposed strict bound.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
N=550172,
\qquad B=17135927,
\qquad v_*=63945.
\]
We will prove that the residue class of \(v_*\) modulo \(N\) is not represented by any \(2^k-k\) with \(1\leq k<B\). It follows that
\[
a(N)\geq B.
\]
We will also give a finite covering argument showing that the defining set for \(a(N)\) is nonempty. Finally, we will show that the \(N\)-th prime is less than \(8567965\). These facts contradict the proposed inequality.

Throughout, congruences without an explicitly stated modulus are modulo \(N\).

## 1. A period for the powers of 2 modulo \(N\)

A modular exponentiation gives
\[
2^{29402}\equiv 4\pmod {550172}.
\]
Consequently, for every integer \(a\geq2\),
\[
2^{a+29400}
 =2^{a-2}2^{29402}
 \equiv 2^{a-2}\cdot4
 =2^a\pmod N.
\]
Iterating this identity gives, for every \(a\geq2\) and every \(t\geq0\),
\[
2^{a+29400t}\equiv2^a\pmod N. \tag{1}
\]
Thus every exponent \(k\geq2\) can be reduced uniquely to the form
\[
k=r+29400t,
\qquad 2\leq r<29402,
\qquad t\geq0, \tag{2}
\]
where explicitly
\[
r=2+((k-2)\bmod29400),
\qquad
 t=\left\lfloor\frac{k-2}{29400}\right\rfloor.
\]
By (1), \(2^k\equiv2^r\pmod N\).

The modular exponentiation above, and all modular exponentiations used below, can be performed by the recurrence
\[
w_2=4,\qquad w_{r+1}\equiv2w_r\pmod N,
\]
so no enormous powers need to be expanded.

## 2. Solving the remaining linear congruence

The factorization relevant to the argument is
\[
550172=196\cdot2807,
\qquad
29400=196\cdot150. \tag{3}
\]
Also,
\[
150\cdot131=19650=7\cdot2807+1, \tag{4}
\]
so \(131\) is the inverse of \(150\) modulo \(2807\).

For integers \(r\geq0\) and \(0\leq v<N\), define the canonical residue
\[
d(r,v)=\bigl((2^r\bmod N)+N-((v+r)\bmod N)\bigr)\bmod N.
\]
Thus \(0\leq d(r,v)<N\), and by construction
\[
d(r,v)\equiv2^r-(v+r)\pmod N. \tag{5}
\]

Suppose first that
\[
2^r\equiv v+r+29400t\pmod N \tag{6}
\]
for some \(t\geq0\). Combining (5) and (6) gives
\[
d(r,v)\equiv29400t\pmod N.
\]
Since both \(29400\) and \(N\) are divisible by \(196\), this implies
\[
196\mid d(r,v).
\]
Write
\[
d(r,v)=196D.
\]
Using (3), the preceding congruence may be divided by \(196\), giving
\[
D\equiv150t\pmod{2807}.
\]
Multiplication by \(131\), using (4), yields
\[
t\equiv131D\pmod{2807}. \tag{7}
\]
Define
\[
\tau(r,v)= (131D)\bmod2807
 =\left(131\frac{d(r,v)}{196}\right)\bmod2807. \tag{8}
\]
This is the least nonnegative integer in the congruence class in (7). Because \(t\geq0\) is in the same class, it follows that
\[
\tau(r,v)\leq t. \tag{9}
\]

Conversely, suppose \(196\mid d(r,v)\), put \(D=d(r,v)/196\), and define \(\tau\) by (8). Then
\[
150\tau\equiv150\cdot131D\equiv D\pmod{2807}.
\]
Multiplying by \(196\), and using (3), gives
\[
29400\tau\equiv196D=d(r,v)\pmod N.
\]
Together with (5), this proves
\[
2^r\equiv v+r+29400\tau\pmod N. \tag{10}
\]
Thus the divisibility condition \(196\mid d(r,v)\) is exactly what is needed to construct an exponent of the form \(r+29400\tau\) representing \(v\).

## 3. The finite avoidance computation for \(v_*=63945\)

For each \(r\) in the single period
\[
2\leq r<29402,
\]
compute
\[
d_r=d(r,63945)
 =\bigl((2^r\bmod N)+N-(63945+r)\bigr)\bmod N. \tag{11}
\]
Here \(63945+r<N\), so no reduction of \(63945+r\) is needed.

The following finite statement results:

> For every \(r\) with \(2\leq r<29402\), either
> \[
> 196\nmid d_r, \tag{12}
> \]
> or, writing
> \[
> \tau_r=\left(131\frac{d_r}{196}\right)\bmod2807,
> \]
> one has
> \[
> B\leq r+29400\tau_r. \tag{13}
> \]

This is a direct finite modular computation. For completeness, it can be reproduced by the following pseudocode:

1. Set \(w=4\), corresponding to \(2^2\bmod N\).
2. For \(r=2,3,\ldots,29401\):
   - set \(d=((w+N-(63945+r))\bmod N)\);
   - check that either \(d\bmod196\neq0\), or
     \[
     r+29400\bigl(((d/196)\cdot131)\bmod2807\bigr)\geq17135927;
     \]
   - replace \(w\) by \(2w\bmod N\).

As useful intermediate check values, the residues \(2^r\bmod N\) at the starts of the successive blocks are
\[
\begin{array}{c|rrrrrrrr}
r&2&1002&2002&3002&4002&5002&6002&7002\\ \hline
2^r\bmod N&4&534136&468372&33688&287120&445916&381756&118700
\end{array}
\]
\[
\begin{array}{c|rrrrrrrr}
r&8002&9002&10002&11002&12002&13002&14002&15002\\ \hline
2^r\bmod N&30480&494036&28876&322408&370528&17648&221356&11232
\end{array}
\]
\[
\begin{array}{c|rrrrrrrr}
r&16002&17002&18002&19002&20002&21002&22002&23002\\ \hline
2^r\bmod N&85016&277496&516492&230980&490828&235792&455540&311180
\end{array}
\]
\[
\begin{array}{c|rrrrrr}
r&24002&25002&26002&27002&28002&29002\\ \hline
2^r\bmod N&269476&208524&288724&67372&40104&423460.
\end{array}
\]
Each entry follows from the preceding one by 1000 applications of doubling modulo \(N\), and the last block ends at \(r=29401\). These block values, together with the stated recurrence, reproduce all 29400 checks (12)–(13).

We now use this finite statement to prove avoidance. Suppose, for a contradiction, that
\[
1\leq k<B
\quad\hbox{and}\quad
2^k-k\equiv63945\pmod N. \tag{14}
\]
Equivalently,
\[
2^k\equiv63945+k\pmod N. \tag{15}
\]
If \(k=1\), then (15) would assert
\[
2\equiv63946\pmod{550172},
\]
which is false. Hence \(k\geq2\).

Write \(k=r+29400t\) as in (2). By the period relation (1), (15) becomes
\[
2^r\equiv63945+r+29400t\pmod N. \tag{16}
\]
The forced-solution calculation of the previous section says that \(196\mid d_r\) and
\[
\tau_r\leq t. \tag{17}
\]
Thus alternative (12) in the finite avoidance computation is impossible, so alternative (13) holds. Therefore
\[
B\leq r+29400\tau_r
   \leq r+29400t
   =k,
\]
contrary to \(k<B\). We have proved:
\[
2^k-k\not\equiv63945\pmod{550172}
\quad(1\leq k<17135927). \tag{18}
\]

## 4. A finite covering argument ensuring that \(a(N)\) exists

Although the lower bound (18) is the part that defeats the proposed inequality, we also establish directly that some finite initial segment covers every residue modulo \(N\).

For each residue \(c\in\{0,1,\ldots,195\}\), choose an exponent \(r_c\) from the following list, whose entries are indexed in order by \(c=0,1,\ldots,195\):
\[
\begin{split}
(&36,143,2,349,308,3,26,225,332,191,50,81,4,31,58,85,48,139,98,193,\\
&220,15,122,237,328,287,146,5,204,311,170,29,60,171,10,37,64,27,118,77,\\
&172,199,226,101,216,307,266,125,72,183,290,149,8,39,150,173,16,43,6,97,\\
&56,151,178,205,80,195,286,245,104,51,162,269,128,475,18,129,152,11,22,49,\\
&76,35,130,157,184,59,174,265,224,83,30,141,248,107,454,413,108,131,330,437,\\
&28,55,14,109,136,163,38,153,244,203,62,9,120,227,86,433,392,87,110,309,416,7,\\
&34,61,88,115,142,17,132,223,182,41,304,99,206,65,412,371,66,89,288,395,254,13,\\
&40,67,94,121,148,111,202,161,20,283,78,185,44,391,350,45,68,267,374,233,12,19,\\
&46,73,100,127,90,181,140,235,262,57,164,23,370,329,24,47,246,353,212,71,102,25,\\
&52,79,106,69,160,119,214,241).
\end{split} \tag{19}
\]
A finite modular exponentiation check gives, for every \(0\leq c<196\),
\[
2\leq r_c<476
\quad\hbox{and}\quad
\bigl((2^{r_c}\bmod N)+N-r_c\bigr)\bmod196=c. \tag{20}
\]
Again, all powers in this table can be reproduced by successive doubling modulo \(N\).

Let \(v\) be any integer with \(0\leq v<N\), put \(c=v\bmod196\), and take \(r=r_c\). Equation (20) says
\[
2^r-r\equiv v\pmod{196},
\]
or equivalently
\[
2^r-(v+r)\equiv0\pmod{196}. \tag{21}
\]
Since \(196\mid N\), the canonical residue \(d(r,v)\), which is congruent to \(2^r-(v+r)\) modulo \(N\), is also congruent to it modulo \(196\). Thus (21) implies
\[
196\mid d(r,v).
\]
The converse construction (10), with
\[
\tau=\left(131\frac{d(r,v)}{196}\right)\bmod2807,
\]
therefore gives
\[
2^r\equiv v+r+29400\tau\pmod N.
\]
Using the period relation (1) once more and setting
\[
k=r+29400\tau,
\]
we obtain
\[
2^k\equiv2^r\equiv v+k\pmod N,
\]
so
\[
2^k-k\equiv v\pmod N.
\]
Moreover, \(r<476\) and \(\tau<2807\), hence
\[
k\leq475+29400\cdot2806=82496875<82526801. \tag{22}
\]
Thus every residue modulo \(N\) is represented by some \(2^k-k\) with \(1\leq k\leq82526801\). In particular, the set of covering indices is nonempty and \(a(N)\) is well-defined.

Now (18) shows that no \(m<B\) can cover every residue: the residue \(63945\) is still missing at every such \(m\). Therefore
\[
a(550172)\geq17135927. \tag{23}
\]
Notice that no assertion about the exact value of \(a(550172)\) is needed.

## 5. Bounding the \(550172\)-nd prime

We next prove the finite prime-counting bound
\[
p_{550172}<8567965. \tag{24}
\]
Here is the sieve calculation underlying it.

Set
\[
X=8567965.
\]
Since
\[
2928^2=8573184>X,
\]
every composite integer \(i<X\) has a prime divisor less than \(2928\): indeed its least prime factor is at most \(\sqrt i<\sqrt X<2928\).

List the primes \(p<2928\), using trial division up to \(\sqrt p\). For every such prime \(p\), mark all multiples
\[
2p,3p,\ldots,
\left\lfloor\frac{X-1}{p}\right\rfloor p.
\]
Taking the union of these marked positions marks every composite integer in \([2,X)\). It may also mark a number more than once, but that is harmless.

A bit-sieve implementation of precisely this operation gives
\[
7,992,566
\]
marked bit positions when the masks are placed in a bit vector of length \(2^{24}=16,777,216\). The population count is obtained by repeatedly summing adjacent binary blocks: first adjacent bits, then adjacent blocks of lengths \(2,4,8,\ldots,2^{23}\). This sequence of pairwise block sums preserves the total number of set bits and ends with the value \(7,992,566\). In particular, at most \(7,992,566\) positions in the smaller interval \([0,X)\) are marked.

There are \(X-2=8,567,963\) integers in \([2,X)\). Hence the number of unmarked integers in this interval is at least
\[
8567963-7992566=575397. \tag{25}
\]
Every unmarked integer in \([2,X)\) is prime, because, as observed above, every composite there has a prime divisor below \(2928\) and was therefore marked. Thus there are at least \(575397\) primes below \(X\). Since
\[
575397>550171,
\]
there are more than \(550171\) primes below \(8567965\), which means that the \(550172\)-nd prime satisfies (24).

(One may obtain a sharper value by a full ordinary sieve, but the weaker bound (24) is already sufficient.)

## 6. Contradiction to the conjectured inequality

From (24), since primes are integers,
\[
p_{550172}\leq8567964.
\]
Therefore
\[
2(p_{550172}-1)
 \leq2(8567964-1)
 =17135926. \tag{26}
\]
Combining (23) and (26) gives
\[
a(550172)
 \geq17135927
 >17135926
 \geq2(p_{550172}-1).
\]
In particular,
\[
a(550172)\not<2(p_{550172}-1).
\]
Thus \(n=550172\) is a counterexample, and the conjecture that
\[
a(n)<2(p_n-1)
\]
for every positive integer \(n\) is false.
